article_title: Massive crowds expected for weekend No Kings protests across state. ‘Standing up for Connecticut’
article_content:
The organizers of the upcoming No Kings Day rallies want potential participants to know they are not alone and to know the plan is to emphasize democratic values in a peaceful way.
This is the message as Connecticut protest leaders are expecting very big numbers, perhaps record-breaking participation for the No Kings Day protests to be held on Saturday March 28. There are more than 3,000 No Kings Day events scheduled across the country and beyond, including nearly 50 to be held in Connecticut.
An estimated 12,000 protesters participated in last October’s No Kings Day protests in Hartford and thousands more gathered throughout the state and millions across the country.
As of Friday, there were about 50 registered rallies planned across Connecticut and organizers are expecting significantly higher turnout than October’s No Kings Day protest worldwide that attracted 7 million people.
Each protest will have unique programming. Organizers said the protests will “elevate democratic values and bring attention to issues affecting immigrant communities, transgender individuals, Black Americans, Muslims, women, LGBTQ people, and other marginalized groups. Organizers also plan to address impacts of current federal policies and U.S. military actions,” according to a No Kings Day statement.
The Hartford No Kings Rally is sponsored by more than two dozen community organizations.
Hartford No Kings Rally organizer Carol Rizzolo, from CT Shoreline Indivisible, said initial estimates were about 15,000 protestors, but in her conversations with State Capitol Police, Hartford is preparing for as many as 20,000.
“I think more and more people are aware of what’s going on and in large part it is affecting them individually,” Rizzolo said. “All of us seeing gas prices go up and all of us are concerned that our sons and daughters or granddaughters and grandsons are going to be going sent overseas to a senseless war.”
“I think that it’s just really impacting people’s lives, who never would have thought they’d be out on the streets, protesting anything,” she added.
The Hartford rally begins at 10 a.m. on the north side of the Connecticut State Capitol at 210 Capitol Ave. Around noon the program will shift to the south side of the property for the activist fair.
Rizzolo said rallies are staggered at different times throughout the state so some people can attend multiple events.
“One is that it absolutely sends a message to other people out there that you’re not alone. We’re all really upset about what’s going on and we are willing to come out on the streets and fight for it,” Rizzolo said. “We won’t accept authoritarian rule, not here. We don’t want to be embarrassed by what our country is doing. What our president is doing, what his administration is doing.”
Rizzolo said the protests are always peaceful and expected speakers include U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Connecticut Attorney General William Tong.
Thousands turn out for CT ‘No Kings’ day rally, lining streets, vowing to protect democracy
She added that the Progressive Women of West Hartford will be dressed in black and holding up signs of names of immigrants who “have been detained or murdered by ICE in detention.”
“The message really is widespread to the congressionals, to the legislators, to the voters. to everybody out there saying we are not putting up with this. There’s always something you can do,” Rizzolo said.
Kica Matos, president of the National Immigration Law Center, will emcee the Hartford protest.
“While we expected harsh immigration enforcement tactics from this administration, the scale of events in Minneapolis was shocking,” Matos said in a statement. “In moments like these, it becomes even more important to stand up for the dignity and safety of every person in our community—regardless of race, ethnicity, religious beliefs, identity, or background.”
“This isn’t about immigrants or one group; it’s about who we are together. It’s about democracy itself. The No Kings Day gathering is a celebration of connection, compassion, and shared responsibility. It reminds us that division doesn’t define us—our commitment to looking out for one another does,” Matos added.
In Farmington, there will be a No Kings pro-democracy rally at the Farmington Town Hall/library/high school campus at 1 Monteith Drive from 1:30 p.m. to 4 p.m.
Riju Das, a civil rights attorney, is organizing the Farmington rally. He said that last June’s No Kings rally drew about 250 and the October No Kings rally drew about 1,000 and is hoping to top that on Saturday.
“It’s a shame that in the United States of America we need to rally against no kings,” Das said. “But currently the federal administration has put us here.”
“This rally is about mobilizing suburban residents in the Farmington Valley,” he added. “We live comfortable private lives and are ignorant to what is happening to our neighbors, because what is happening to them could happen to us.”
The Farmington events start at 1:30 p.m. an hour and a half after the Hartford rally, for those who want to attend both.
Das said state legislators have shown up to speak in the past but as of Saturday a list of speakers had not been finalized.
In New Haven, the rally and march will be held at 3 p.m. on the New Haven Green. The rally is headed by Nan Becker, the founder of Greater Westville Indivisible.
The New Haven rally will be held from 3 to 5:30 p.m. Becker also held the No Kings rally in the city in October. Becker estimated that between 5,000 and 6,000 people gathered at the October rally and is hoping for more on Saturday.
She said the goal is connect with community organizations and she said there will be more than 30 at Saturday’s rally. She said the rally will feature speakers and some musical activities as well.
“The good news is that there are Indivisible rallies planned across the state. We’re really here saying, yes, we’re standing up for Connecticut and if you’re in New Haven or in the area of New Haven, come on over. But please stand up wherever you are.”
Becker, a climate activist, said there are a variety of reasons that protestors are choosing to attend her rally including for no kings, no foreign wars for oil, the environment, affordability, dignity for immigrant rights.
“No Kings is a chance to give everyone a voice,” Becker said. “There is a hope for a real connection for those who want to take action for a better future.”
“The No. 1 fundamental of the rally is that it is peaceful, and we ask that of all of our rallygoers,” she said. “Our organizers are asked to follow de-escalation training to make sure we don’t engage in anything that could result in a bad outcome. Peaceful, joyful, cynicism, skepticism, and laughter are our friends.”
Mary-Joan Forstbauer is running the No Kings protest in New Britain. It will be held in front of city hall from 1 to 3 p.m.
This is Forstbauer’s first time running a rally. She is hoping for 200 but isn’t positive about how many to expect and which speakers are expected.
“We’re looking for a joyful celebration of our democracy and first amendment rights to speak out against the Trump administration,” Forstbauer said. “I wanted New Britain to have a place on the map to have a voice in the state and in the nation. I felt strongly about organizing one in New Britain and have a lot of support.”
Charla Nich, a member of CT Shoreline Indivisible, said protest numbers have grown since last year. She said at the Hands-Off national protest in April 2025 had 1,400 rallies across the nation, the No Kings rally last June featured 1,800 protests and No Kings 2 in October had 2,700 total protests nationwide.
“We have created this system to do peaceful protests simultaneously. A lot of it is in reaction to the invasion and the callous treatment of people at the hands of ICE and other agents in Minneapolis. And we know it’s not going to end. The chaos just continues and they continue to marginalize and divide,” Nich said.
